sections.notes:
I opened all five source pages (A06 to A10 on top10.owasp.org/2025). Each returned HTTP 200 and is the current 2025 Final text. The source supports every answer as stated, so there is no wrong_answer. Cards that pass: sr3-01, 03, 05, 07, 10, 11.

Section-level issue: in the original set, every false card says the category endorses a bad practice and every true card says it recommends a good one. A player who guesses 'OWASP recommends the sensible thing' scores 12/12, which breaks the no-wording-tells rule. The replacements above use scope and mapping misconceptions instead, to break that pattern. sr3-10 ('keeps logs solely on the app server') still follows the pattern but rests on a realistic misconception, so I let it pass.

Borderline passes:
- sr3-01: threat modeling under Insecure Design is close to a name-level guess, but it is OWASP's own How-to-prevent item.
- sr3-07: 'uses signatures to verify updates' is guessable from 'Integrity'.

Overlap to watch: the A03:2025 page also covers 'components from untrusted sources' and 'Prefer signed packages (see A08...)'. sr3-06 and sr3-07 are therefore phrased correctly as A08 statements, but must never be inverted into 'only A08' claims.

Proposed replacements keep the 6 true / 6 false balance and stay within 120/240 characters (statements 103 to 118, explanations 167 to 183). No replacement duplicates sr3-11 (rollback/fail closed), sr3-05 (new session ID after login) or the r2 mappings. The A10 page's own wording 'One application should not multiple functions...' is garbled in the source, which is another reason to keep A10 cards away from the local-versus-global handler question.

A definition that considers the scheme is sometimes called a schemeful same-site." The source supports the answer, but the term itself gives it away.

The false statement is only false by the meaning of its own name. It is also browser-dependent: the prompt's trap (f) says it applies in some browsers only, yet volatility is "stable".

Explanation: "A site is set by the registrable domain and the port plays no part, so both URLs are the same site even though they are different origins." Source: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Site ("These are considered the same site because the port number is ignored when determining the site").

flagged.evidence: MDN SOP: "Cross-origin reads are typically disallowed" and "Use CORS to allow cross-origin access." A cross-origin 200 response that carries a matching Access-Control-Allow-Origin does expose its body to fetch(). The statement never says CORS headers are missing.
flagged.problem: The statement reads as "a cross-origin fetch() exposes its body when the server returns 200". For any CORS-enabled API that is true, so an expert could defend True. The intended fact, that the status code alone does not grant a read, needs the word "alone" or a similar qualifier. The explanation is also two sentences that mostly repeat each other.
flagged.suggestedFix: Keep false. Statement: "A 200 status alone lets script read the body of a cross-origin fetch() response." Explanation: "The status code is irrelevant: the same-origin policy keeps a cross-origin response body from script unless the response passes the CORS check." Do not name Access-Control-Allow-Origin, so it stays clear of r5-01.

flagged.evidence: MDN SOP: "Cross-origin writes are typically allowed. Examples are links, redirects, and form submissions." This supports the card. But web-security-sr9-01 (true) says "A cross-site form can make a server act under the victim's session cookie when the cookie is sent."

flagged.suggestedFix: Replace with a true card on a different origin fact (answer: true). Statement: "Modern browsers usually give a document opened from a file:/// URL an opaque origin." Explanation: "The URL spec leaves file origins to each browser, and most treat them as opaque, so a local page that loads a sibling file can hit a CORS error." Source: same MDN SOP page, File origins section ("Modern browsers usually treat the origin of files loaded using the file:/// scheme as opaque origins").

flagged.problem: This is a definition card: it restates what "origin" means, so anyone who knows the term answers True and nobody learns how the tuple behaves. It also has edge cases (an opaque origin, such as a sandboxed iframe, can have a matching scheme, host and port), and the explanation's "for network URLs" points at them without saying what they are.

sections.notes:
I opened both source URLs (MDN Same-origin policy and MDN Glossary/Site). Both return 200 and are current MDN pages, and I read their full current source text. Cards 02, 03, 06, 08, 09, 10, 11 and 12 pass. Evidence for each:
- 02: "If this popup also contains JavaScript, that script would inherit the same origin as the script that created it."
- 08 and 09: the cross-origin table lists window.closed as "Read only." and location.href as "Write-only.".
- 10: "To communicate between documents from different origins, use window.postMessage."
- 11: "Web Storage and IndexedDB are separated by origin."
- 12: changing document.domain "does not affect the origin checks used by many Web APIs (e.g., localStorage, indexedDB ...)". The statement is also false in current Chrome, where the setter does nothing by default because agent clusters are origin-keyed.

Minor observations, not flagged:
- 02: with window.open(..., "noopener") the initial about:blank document gets an opaque origin. The statement's "script-created" popup (one the script holds a reference to) excludes that case, but an expert might raise it.
- 06: an easy false card that is close to a strawman for working frontend developers. I kept it because confusing CORS with ordinary image embedding is a real misconception.
- 03: uses the hedge "can" on a true card. That is acceptable, because public-suffix hosts such as github.io make sibling subdomains different sites.
- Overlap checks: 07 is close to r5-01 (Access-Control-Allow-Origin); the suggested fix keeps the explanation generic. 04's replacement (site ignores the port) and 01's replacement (default port within the origin) test different facts.

True/false balance: the section stays at 6 true and 6 false with all four fixes. Average statement length becomes 77.3 characters for true and 77.5 for false.

MDN CORS guide: "The only type/subtype combinations allowed for the media type specified in the Content-Type header are: application/x-www-form-urlencoded multipart/form-data text/plain". The problem is that web-security-sr9-06 ("Content-Type: application/json makes a cross-origin fetch() POST skip preflight.", false, "application/json is outside the Content-Type values that avoid CORS preflight") tests the other side of the same safelisted Content-Type split. Prompt rule: "The two sides of one distinction are one fact."

Statement: "Access-Control-Max-Age sets how long a browser may cache the actual response of a CORS request." (answer false, 95 chars). Explanation: "Access-Control-Max-Age sets how long a browser may cache a preflight result, so later matching requests skip a new preflight. Each browser caps the value at its own maximum." Misconception: Max-Age caches the response like Cache-Control. Source: same CORS guide ("Access-Control-Max-Age gives the value in seconds for how long the response to the preflight request can be cached without sending another preflight request").

It is also a close pair with sr5-06 (Request-Method on the request side, Allow-Methods on the response side), and both are true.

Explanation: "A per-origin Access-Control-Allow-Origin makes the response differ by Origin, and Vary: Origin tells caches to store a separate copy for each requesting origin." The statement "Access-Control-Expose-Headers lets JavaScript read named response headers beyond the safelist" is the header name in sentence form, and a hedge verb ("lets") marks it as true.

I checked all 12 r10 cards (6 true, 6 false) against the MDN Clickjacking, X-Frame-Options and frame-ancestors pages, which all return 200 and are current (modified Feb 2 2026, Sep 17 2026 and Aug 27 2026). I also checked them against CSP Level 3.

Confirmed:
- sr10-05: MDN says "A policy that declares default-src 'none' still allows the resource to be embedded by anyone."
- sr10-08: MDN says SAMEORIGIN "can only be embedded if all ancestor frames have the same origin".
- sr10-09: MDN says ALLOW-FROM is obsolete and "Modern browsers ... will ignore the header completely".
- sr10-10: MDN says setting XFO in a meta element "has no effect".

Fix proposals:

- The sr10-06 replacement uses a meta-element pattern that sr10-10 and sr8-11 also use as false statements. The replacement is true, so it does not add a third false use of that template.

sections.notes:
All 12 r11 cards cite https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Defenses/Subresource_Integrity, which loads (200, last modified Apr 14, 2026) and supports each card as written. I also checked the cards against the SRI spec at https://www.w3.org/TR/sri/ (now the SRI Level 2 Working Draft), the WHATWG HTML script element and the MDN crossorigin page.

Section balance is 6 true and 6 false (false: 01, 03, 04, 07, 11, 12). All three replacements are false, so the balance holds. With them, difficulty becomes 4 easy, 5 medium, 3 hard.

Passed, with minor remarks:
- 02 (sha256/sha384/sha512): correct. The spec's valid token set is exactly these three.
- 03 (hex encoding): correct. The spec defines the digest as base64 encoded, and CSP's base64-value grammar also allows base64url characters. A hex string is syntactically valid base64 but never matches, so the false answer holds.
- 04: the strongest-algorithm rule is quoted on MDN: "it will only use the hashes generated using SHA-384. It will ignore all other hashes."
- 05: correct. Small nit: if a sha512 hash were also listed, the two sha384 hashes would be ignored. Optional tightening: "With only two sha384- hashes listed, the browser accepts a resource matching either."
- 06: correct. crossorigin="use-credentials" also gives CORS mode, but the statement does not claim exclusivity.
- 08: the network error on a mismatch is quoted on MDN and in SRI spec section 3.7.
- 10 (stylesheet, preload, modulepreload): correct per MDN ("<link> elements whose rel attribute value is stylesheet, preload, or modulepreload"). It follows MDN's list closely, but it is a list fact rather than a copied sentence.

Overlap check against the rest of the deck: sr8-04 (a CSP hash breaks after a whitespace edit) already uses the "hash still matches after content changes" template, so the sr11-01 replacement avoids it. The crossorigin-anonymous replacement for sr11-11 tests the HTML attribute's credentials mode, which is a different fact from sr5-08 (what Access-Control-Allow-Credentials controls). I did not use an inline-script replacement (the HTML script attribute table does not allow integrity on inline scripts), because it is the other side of sr11-09's "<script src>" fact.

That qualifier only makes sense because of the IP-host exception, so 03 and 05 are the two sides of one domain-versus-IP split, and 03 gives away 05.

Explanation: "Mixed content covers insecure subresource requests from a secure context. A top-level navigation to an HTTP URL creates a new context, so it is not mixed content." (162 chars). Same URL; MDN: "navigation requests from a secure context that target insecure target top-level browsing contexts are not considered mixed content". factKey mixed-content-navigation-excluded, volatility may_change (HTTPS-first browser modes).

The same page also says: "Requests using GET or HEAD, or made in cors, websocket, or webtransport mode, are never affected."

A cross-origin fetch() with mode "no-cors" and method POST under no-referrer sends Origin: null, so the referrer policy does remove the origin value. With "can" in the statement, an expert could defend True. The explanation adds a CORS-mode condition that the statement never states.

Explanation: "Requests in cors mode always carry their real origin in Origin, whatever the referrer policy. no-referrer turns Origin into null only for non-GET requests in other modes, such as form posts." (190 chars). Same URL.

The fact is correct.

That cross-origin leak is why strict-origin-when-cross-origin replaced it as the default." (186 chars). Same URL.

(157 chars). Same URL; MDN: "To disable HSTS, set max-age=0."

But it does not apply to example.com or insecure.example.com." The fact is correct.

The card also mirrors MDN's own example. MDN describes a real and less obvious limit of includeSubDomains: it does nothing until the browser has received the parent's header.

Same URL; MDN: "if example.com includes the HSTS header with includeSubDomains, but all existing links go directly to www.example.com, the browser will never see example.com's HSTS header."

The fact is correct (RFC 6797 section 8.1).

flagged.suggestedFix: Reword and keep the answer true. Statement: "Only a Strict-Transport-Security header received over HTTPS adds a host to the browser's HSTS list." (99 chars, answer true; MDN says "The host must send the Strict-Transport-Security header over HTTPS only"). Explanation: "A header on a plain-HTTP response could be forged or stripped by a network attacker, so browsers discard it and act only on HSTS headers delivered over HTTPS." (158 chars). Same URL.

sections.notes:
I checked all 12 r12 cards. The section is balanced 6 true and 6 false, and every suggested replacement keeps the answer of the card it replaces. All four source URLs returned 200 on 2026-10-03. I read them as the MDN source markdown (mdn/content main).

Cards that pass:
- sr12-01: MDN, Framed documents: an https iframe in an http parent is "Not secure".
- sr12-02: the MDN table shows http://localhost as "Secure (localhost URL)".
- sr12-03: MDN says img src with a domain-name host is upgradable. The MDN browser compatibility data (BCD) still lists Safari auto_upgrade_images as false, but WebKit's Safari 18.0 release notes (https://webkit.org/blog/15865/webkit-features-in-safari-18-0/) say images, video and audio are now auto-upgraded. The true answer holds in current Chrome, Firefox (127 and later) and Safari, and may_change is right.
- sr12-04: script src is blockable. One edge: a CSP upgrade-insecure-requests directive would upgrade the script, but the statement describes default behaviour, so that is acceptable.
- sr12-09: MDN, \"Preloading mitigates this problem\" about the first-visit weakness.
- sr12-10: MDN, strict-origin-when-cross-origin \"(default)\" sends the origin only for cross-origin HTTPS to HTTPS.

Minor style point, not flagged: sr12-03 and sr12-04 say \"An HTTPS page upgrades\" where the browser is the actor. A rewrite such as \"On an HTTPS page, the browser upgrades ...\" would follow the name-the-actor rule better.

Duplicate search across b1 to b3: no other card tests HSTS, mixed content, secure contexts or Referrer-Policy. The only related card is sr2-11 (a04-hsts-versus-tls), an OWASP mapping card, and none of the r12 cards or replacements repeats it.

Not used as a replacement: a card on the HSTS preload directive not being part of RFC 6797 is a free, untested fact the prompt lists as a trap. It could stand in for sr12-07 if the www.example.com version is not wanted.

duplicates.why: Both test which Content-Type values are CORS-safelisted on a cross-origin fetch() POST: text/plain avoids a preflight, application/json triggers one. These are the two sides of one distinction, so knowing one answers the other. sr5-04 is weaker: its clause 'because of that Content-Type' is clumsy and its misconception ('any explicit Content-Type triggers a preflight') is close to a strawman.

Same fact, both false on the same 'matching hash is enough' trick: cross-origin SRI needs a CORS-enabled response, and a matching digest cannot replace Access-Control-Allow-Origin or rescue an opaque no-cors response. sr11-11 is the more opaque wording of the two.

If a digest mismatch gives a network error and the resource is refused (sr11-08), the script cannot run before the check (sr11-12). sr11-12 is close to a strawman: nobody who studied SRI thinks it checks after execution.

Two sides of one distinction: React escapes interpolated JSX text, and dangerouslySetInnerHTML does not. sr7-10's explanation ('without applying normal output encoding') gives sr7-09 away. The prompt also allows at most one framework escape-hatch card, so sr7-09 breaks that rule.

Mirrored true/false pair with almost the same wording ('frame-ancestors X permits a same-origin page to embed the protected page'): 'none' is false, 'self' is true. One fact about same-origin framing, and sr10-04 can be read off the keyword 'self', so it is close to a definition card.

The upgradable (img) versus blockable (script) mixed-content split is one two-way distinction. sr12-03's qualifier 'at a domain-name URL' also leaks sr12-05 (the IP-address exception), and sr12-05's explanation already teaches the normal image upgrade.

scan.tells:
Statement length is balanced: in every section the true and false averages are within 5 characters (largest gap 4.3, in r1 and r3; overall true 84.7, false 85.5). False explanations run 15 to 31 characters longer in r1, r4, r5, r6 and r7, but the player only sees them after answering. The exploitable tells are wording and polarity:

1. OWASP polarity in r1 to r3, the strongest tell. True cards have OWASP prescribe a control or list a weakness. False cards have OWASP endorse a lax or naive stance, usually with an unusual verb. a) "includes" in r2: 6 True (sr2-02, 04, 05, 06, 09, 12), 1 False (sr2-03). b) "calls for": 3 True (sr3-01, 09, 11), 0 False. c) Strawman false stances: sr2-01 "lets client-side route guards secure API access", sr2-08 "limits inventory to direct dependencies", sr2-10 "recommends caching sensitive responses", sr2-11 "uses HSTS as the cipher", sr3-02 "finds flawless code sufficient", sr3-04 "equates a cleared login screen with session invalidation", sr3-06 "counts a CDN download as verification", sr3-08 "trusts serialized data that parses", sr3-10 "keeps logs solely on the app server", plus sr1-01. Rule a non-expert can use: "would a security guide recommend something lax? No, so False." That answers about 10 of the 12 false cards in r2 and r3. Only sr2-03, sr2-07 and sr3-12 need knowledge.

2. Rank specificity in r1. Cards with exact ranks are True: sr1-04 "fifth to second", sr1-08 "fourth to sixth", sr1-10 "stays at eighth". Cards with only a vague direction are False: sr1-06 "moves higher than its 2021 rank", sr1-07 "keeps its 2021 ranking". The rule predicts 5 of 5.

3. Limiting, additive and contrast words mark False: 14 occurrences, all in false statements, none in true ones. "also" ×3 (sr4-12, sr6-09, sr10-11), "solely" (sr3-10), "fully" (sr9-11), "just" (sr10-08), "alone" (sr7-07), "still" (sr8-04), "even" (sr11-04), "both" (sr8-10), "excludes" (sr6-03), "skip" (sr9-06), "rather than" (sr11-01), "replaces" ×2 (sr9-11, sr11-07).

4. Verb skew. "requires": 3 False (sr6-09, sr7-01, sr7-03), 1 True (sr6-07); the prompt says requirement words must not mark false statements. "makes": 4 False (sr5-08, sr7-06, sr9-06, sr10-10), 1 True (sr8-01). "blocks": 4 False (sr4-06, sr6-12, sr8-08, sr10-05), 1 True (sr10-07). "permits": 3 True (sr4-05, sr8-07, sr10-04), 1 False (sr10-03). "In supporting browsers": 3 True (sr6-10, sr7-11, sr8-12), 1 False (sr6-11). "can" leans the other way, 9 False and 6 True, which is fine as hedge balance.

5. Recurring false templates. "A matching hash suffices despite X" carries 3 false cards (sr11-04, sr11-07, sr11-11), over the limit of 2; r11 then reads as "matching-hash claims are False" (3 of 4, with sr11-05 the only True). "X XSS requires Y": sr7-01 and sr7-03, both False. "A meta element delivers/makes X effective": sr8-11 and sr10-10, both False, at the limit. "Category wrongly filed under Authentication Failures": sr2-03 and sr2-07, both False, at the limit. Same-template true/false pairs a player can contrast: "An HTTPS page upgrades an HTTP ..." (sr12-03 True, sr12-04 and sr12-05 False); "A script can read X on a Window from another origin" (sr4-08 True, sr4-09 False); "frame-ancestors 'none'/'self' permits a same-origin page" (sr10-03 False, sr10-04 True); "The same-origin policy typically permits/blocks" (sr4-05 True, sr4-06 False).

6. Name and definition giveaways. True cards where a header or keyword describes itself: sr5-01 (Access-Control-Allow-Origin), sr5-05 (Access-Control-Request-Method), sr5-06 (Access-Control-Allow-Methods), sr5-07 (Access-Control-Allow-Headers), sr5-10 (Access-Control-Expose-Headers), sr12-06 (HSTS max-age = how long), sr10-04 ('self'). In r5, 5 of the 7 statements that open with a header name are True; only sr5-08 and sr5-09 are False. False cards contradicted by their own name: sr8-08 (Report-Only "blocks"), sr7-10 ("dangerously" SetInnerHTML "sanitizes"), sr4-04 ("schemeful" ignores scheme), sr10-03 ('none' permits), sr12-12 (no-referrer-when-downgrade on a non-downgrade), sr10-09 ("obsolete" ALLOW-FROM, enforced by modern browsers).

7. Truism and strawman cards. sr10-06 (True): the statement only says frame-ancestors works in a header; the tested meta fact appears only in the explanation. sr9-07 (False): a custom-header defence that accepts requests without the header. sr11-12, sr2-10, sr1-01 and sr3-04 (False): nobody who studied would answer True.

Other observations, not tells:
- Volatility. sr6-11 (Partitioned), sr7-11 and sr8-12 (Trusted Types) and sr4-04 (schemeful same-site) are marked "stable", but the prompt rules (d), (e) and (f) require "may_change".
- sr7-09 is a second React API card, against the one-escape-hatch limit.
- sr2-07's statement "assigns a missing HttpOnly flag to authentication" is muddled wording.
- Checked against top10.owasp.org today: A02:2025 maps CWE-1004 and lists stack traces, and A01:2025 maps CWE-352 and covers CORS misconfiguration and server-side enforcement. So sr2-01, sr2-03, sr2-04, sr2-06 and sr2-07 are factually supported.
